name: Triangle Choke
description: Learn Triangle Choke from Crackhead Control in BJJ. Step-by-step setup from turtle bottom to Triangle Control. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Triangle Choke from Crackhead Control is an advanced submission setup that exploits the unique mechanics of the 10th Planet turtle bottom position. When the top player commits to controlling the upper body from Crackhead Control, the bottom player's constant hip movement and aggressive hand fighting can create openings to shoot a leg across the opponent's neck and trap one arm inside, transitioning directly into Triangle Control. This attack capitalizes on the opponent's forward weight commitment and grip-seeking behavior, turning their offensive pressure into a submission vulnerability.

Strategically, this triangle entry represents one of the highest-value attacks available from Crackhead Control bottom because it transforms a defensive survival position into an immediate finishing threat. The mechanics differ from traditional closed guard triangle setups in several key ways: the angle of entry comes from underneath and behind rather than from a supine position, the initial leg placement must account for the opponent's chair-sit weight distribution, and the transition requires an explosive inversion or rotation to secure the triangle configuration. The entry window typically opens when the opponent reaches across the body for grip changes or commits weight forward to flatten the turtle.

This technique exemplifies the modern grappling principle that defensive positions should always carry offensive potential. The frenetic energy of Crackhead Control bottom creates unpredictable scramble dynamics where the opponent's pattern recognition breaks down. By threading a leg through during these chaotic exchanges, the bottom player bypasses the opponent's defensive reactions entirely - they are focused on maintaining top control, not defending submissions from someone they believe is in an inferior position. The surprise factor alone significantly increases the success rate at all skill levels compared to more telegraphed triangle entries.
key_principles: Explosive hip rotation is essential to create the angle needed to shoot the leg across the opponent's neck from turtle bottom position
Timing the entry to coincide with opponent's grip transitions or weight shifts maximizes success probability and minimizes defensive reaction time
The inside leg must clear the opponent's shoulder line before the triangle can be locked, requiring precise spatial awareness of opponent's posture
Arm isolation happens simultaneously with leg insertion - the attacking leg must trap one arm inside while excluding the other
Maintaining head control throughout the transition prevents the opponent from posturing out before the triangle lock is consolidated
The rotation from turtle to supine triangle position must be continuous and explosive to prevent the opponent from basing out or disengaging
setup_requirements: Opponent committed to Crackhead Control top with forward weight distribution and active grip seeking on upper body
Bottom player has maintained hip mobility and is not flattened to the mat with both hooks established
At least one of the opponent's arms is extended or reaching across the body, creating space between their elbow and torso
Bottom player has sufficient space between their shoulder and the opponent's chest to thread a leg through the gap
Opponent's head is positioned forward past their hips, creating vulnerability to leg entanglement around the neck

execution_steps.description: From Crackhead Control bottom, monitor the opponent's grip patterns and weight shifts. The optimal moment occurs when they reach across your body with one arm to establish a new grip or when they shift weight forward to flatten you - this creates the space needed between their arm and torso.

Drive your near-side hip explosively upward and toward the opponent while simultaneously rotating your body to face them. This hip bump disrupts their chair-sit base and creates the angle necessary to shoot your leg across their neck. Use your posted hands to redirect your body's momentum into the rotation.

Shoot your far-side leg across the back of the opponent's neck, threading it between their head and the arm that is extended or isolated. The shin should contact the back of the neck with your knee pointing toward their trapped shoulder. Your calf must clear their shoulder line completely to establish the choking angle.

As your leg crosses the neck, use your same-side hand to control the opponent's trapped arm, pulling it across their own centerline. The arm must stay inside the triangle while the opposite arm remains outside. Grip their wrist or forearm and pull it tight against your hip to prevent them from extracting the arm.

Bring your other leg up and hook the ankle of your choking leg behind your opposite knee, creating the figure-four triangle lock. Squeeze your knees together while pulling the opponent's head down with your hands on the back of their skull. Your hips should begin elevating to increase compression on the carotid arteries.

Rotate your body approximately 30-45 degrees perpendicular to the opponent's centerline by walking your shoulders on the mat. This angle adjustment directs your choking knee toward their trapped shoulder, optimizing arterial compression. Pull the trapped arm across their neck and elevate your hips off the mat using your upper back as a base point.

With the triangle locked, angle adjusted, and hips elevated, you have transitioned from Crackhead Control bottom into full Triangle Control. From here, maintain constant downward head pressure and hip elevation to prevent posture recovery while threatening the choke finish, armbar transitions, or omoplata switches based on the opponent's defensive reactions.

common_counters.counter: Opponent postures up explosively before the triangle lock is consolidated, stacking weight onto the bottom player's shoulders to create space and prevent the lock from closing
common_counters.your_response: Transition to omoplata by uncrossing your ankles and rotating your hips, using the opponent's posture against them. Alternatively, switch to armbar by swinging your leg over their head while maintaining arm control.

common_counters.counter: Opponent extracts the trapped arm by turning their elbow inward and pulling sharply before the triangle is fully locked, removing the submission threat
common_counters.your_response: If both arms come inside, immediately transition to closed guard or overhook guard. If both arms come outside, re-attack with a wider triangle or switch to armbar on the now-extended arm.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward and stacks the bottom player, walking their feet toward the head to compress the spine and relieve triangle pressure
common_counters.your_response: Frame on their hip with your hands to prevent full stack completion. Use shoulder walking to re-angle your body perpendicular to their drive, converting their forward pressure into lateral exposure for a tighter choke angle.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bases out wide with their free hand and circles away from the choking leg, creating distance to posture and begin systematic escape
common_counters.your_response: Control their posture by pulling their head down with overhook or collar tie grip. If they create distance, release the triangle and transition to armbar on the posted arm or switch to back take by following their rotation.

common_errors.error: Attempting the triangle without sufficient hip rotation, trying to thread the leg from a flat turtle position
common_errors.consequence: The leg cannot clear the opponent's shoulder line, resulting in a loose half-triangle that the opponent easily shrugs off while maintaining top control
common_errors.correction: Commit to explosive hip rotation before attempting to thread the leg. Your body must be facing the opponent with hips elevated before the leg can cross their neck at the correct angle.

common_errors.error: Failing to isolate one arm inside the triangle, allowing both of the opponent's arms to remain on the same side of the choking leg
common_errors.consequence: No choking pressure is generated because the opponent can use both hands to frame and create space, turning the triangle into a loose headlock with no submission threat
common_errors.correction: Prioritize arm isolation simultaneously with leg insertion. Use your near-side hand to pull one arm across while your leg threads over the neck. One arm in, one arm out is non-negotiable for triangle mechanics.

common_errors.error: Locking the triangle with incorrect leg configuration - hooking the ankle behind the wrong knee or crossing ankles instead of figure-four
common_errors.consequence: Dramatically reduced choking pressure and increased risk of the opponent slipping their head free. Crossed ankles create a footlock vulnerability rather than a choke.
common_errors.correction: The choking leg's ankle must hook behind the opposite knee in a figure-four configuration. The knee of the choking leg points toward the trapped arm's shoulder. Practice the lock configuration in isolation until it becomes automatic.

common_errors.error: Neglecting the perpendicular angle adjustment after locking the triangle, remaining square to the opponent
common_errors.consequence: Reduced arterial compression by approximately 40-50%, allowing the opponent to breathe and defend while systematically working their escape sequence
common_errors.correction: After locking the triangle, immediately walk your shoulders to create a 30-45 degree angle relative to the opponent's centerline. Your choking knee should point toward their trapped shoulder, not straight up.

common_errors.error: Telegraphing the triangle attempt by pausing hip movement before the explosive entry, alerting the opponent to the attack
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the setup and preemptively withdraws their arm or flattens you, eliminating the entry window and potentially advancing to back control
common_errors.correction: The triangle entry must emerge from the continuous hip movement of Crackhead Control bottom. Never pause or reset before attacking - the entry should be a seamless acceleration of existing movement patterns.

common_errors.error: Releasing head control after locking the triangle, allowing the opponent to posture up and begin stacking
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates space to breathe, begins systematic stack passing, and may extract the trapped arm to fully escape the triangle position
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant downward pressure on the back of the opponent's head with both hands immediately after locking the triangle. Head control is the primary mechanism preventing posture recovery.

training_progressions.description: Practice the hip rotation and leg threading motion from turtle bottom against a stationary partner. Focus on the mechanical pathway: hip bump, rotation, leg across neck, arm isolation, lock. Drill each component separately then chain them together. No resistance - partner holds Crackhead Control top position and allows the entry.

Partner provides light movement from Crackhead Control top, reaching for grips and shifting weight. Bottom player identifies entry windows based on arm extensions and weight transfers, then executes the full triangle entry sequence. Focus on recognizing the three primary triggers: cross-body reach, weight shift forward, and grip transition moments.

Partner provides medium resistance, attempting to posture out, stack, and extract the trapped arm after the triangle is locked. Bottom player works angle adjustment, hip elevation, and transitions to armbar or omoplata when the triangle defense is effective. Develop the ability to flow between triangle, armbar, and omoplata based on defensive reactions.

training_progressions.focus: Integration with Crackhead Control bottom game
training_progressions.description: Full positional sparring from Crackhead Control bottom. Triangle entry becomes one option among granby rolls, sit-throughs, and guard recoveries. Partner provides full resistance from top. Bottom player selects attacks based on what the opponent gives them. Track triangle entry success rate and compare with other escape/attack options.

Integrate triangle from Crackhead Control into full rolling sessions. Work on setting up the position through deliberate turtle recovery after guard passes, then attacking with the triangle when the opponent follows to Crackhead Control top. Develop the psychological aspect - maintaining composure in bottom turtle while hunting for submission entries.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of rotating to face the opponent, invert underneath them by shooting your hips through and threading the triangle from an inverted position. This variation works when the opponent maintains heavy forward pressure that prevents the standard hip rotation, using their own weight commitment to create the submission angle.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent drives forward aggressively and your hip rotation is blocked by their chest pressure

variants_and_adaptations.description: Secure an overhook on the opponent's near arm before initiating the triangle entry. The overhook provides arm isolation prior to the leg insertion, reducing the need for simultaneous arm control and leg threading. This simplifies the entry by separating the arm isolation from the leg mechanics into two distinct phases.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you can establish an overhook during the grip fighting phase of Crackhead Control bottom before committing to the triangle

variants_and_adaptations.description: Execute a forward or sideways roll from turtle position, using the rolling momentum to carry your legs over the opponent's head and neck. The roll creates space and angle simultaneously, and the opponent's reaction to the unexpected motion often exposes their arm for isolation. This is the highest-risk but most unpredictable entry.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against opponents who maintain very tight control and deny standard hip rotation, particularly when they sit back rather than drive forward

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of the Triangle Choke from Crackhead Control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to transition from the defensive Crackhead Control bottom position into Triangle Control, a dominant submission platform. This converts a survival position into an immediate finishing threat by threading a leg across the opponent's neck while isolating one arm inside, establishing the figure-four triangle lock that compresses the carotid arteries.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the three primary triggers that create an entry window for this triangle from Crackhead Control bottom?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The three primary triggers are: (1) the opponent reaches across your body with one arm to establish a new grip, creating space between their elbow and torso; (2) the opponent shifts weight forward to flatten you, bringing their head past their hips; and (3) the opponent transitions between grip configurations, creating a momentary gap in their control structure. All three involve the opponent committing to an action that temporarily opens their neck to leg entry.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent postures up immediately after you lock the triangle - how do you adjust your attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: First attempt to break their posture by pulling their head down with both hands on the back of the skull. If they maintain posture, transition to omoplata by uncrossing your ankles, rotating your hips 180 degrees, and controlling their arm in the omoplata configuration. Alternatively, if their posturing extends their trapped arm, pivot to an armbar by swinging your choking leg over their head while maintaining wrist control. The triangle, armbar, and omoplata form a triangle of attacks where defending one exposes the other.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the critical mechanical detail in the hip rotation that initiates this triangle entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The near-side hip must drive upward and toward the opponent explosively, not just laterally. This hip bump simultaneously disrupts the opponent's chair-sit base and creates the angle for your far-side leg to thread across their neck. The rotation should originate from the core, not the shoulders - turning your shoulders without hip engagement creates insufficient space for leg insertion. Your posted hands redirect momentum into the rotation rather than generating it.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must the perpendicular angle adjustment happen after locking the triangle, and what is the optimal angle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The angle adjustment (30-45 degrees relative to the opponent's centerline) is essential because a square triangle compresses the front of the neck (trachea) rather than the sides (carotid arteries). The perpendicular angle directs the choking knee toward the trapped arm's shoulder, creating a diagonal compression vector that targets both carotid arteries simultaneously. Without this angle, the choke becomes an air choke requiring significantly more force, giving the opponent substantially more time to escape.

knowledge_assessment.question: What grip configuration is required for the trapped arm, and why does arm positioning matter for choke pressure?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The trapped arm must be pulled across the opponent's own neck so that their shoulder and bicep compress one side of their neck while your thigh compresses the other side. Grip their wrist or forearm with your same-side hand and pull it tight against your hip. This arm positioning is critical because the opponent's own limb becomes a lever that amplifies choking pressure - without proper arm positioning across the centerline, the triangle becomes a head squeeze rather than a blood choke, dramatically reducing effectiveness.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent begins stacking you by driving forward and walking their feet toward your head - what is your defensive response?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Frame on their hip with both hands to arrest their forward drive and prevent full spinal compression. Simultaneously, use shoulder walking to angle your body perpendicular to their drive direction - this converts their linear forward pressure into a lateral exposure that actually improves your choking angle. If the stack progresses despite framing, release the triangle temporarily, push their hips back with your feet, and immediately re-establish the triangle from the new angle. Never absorb a full stack passively.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does this triangle entry differ mechanically from a standard closed guard triangle, and what adjustment is required?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The standard closed guard triangle enters from a supine position with the opponent above you, threading the leg from front to back. The Crackhead Control triangle enters from turtle bottom, requiring a rotation from prone to supine position during the entry. This means the initial leg path goes from underneath and behind rather than from in front, requiring explosive hip rotation to create the entry angle. The adjustment is committing fully to the rotation before attempting leg insertion - half-committed entries from turtle result in loose positions that are easily shrugged off.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the chain attack options if the opponent successfully defends the initial triangle lock?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the opponent prevents the triangle from fully locking: (1) switch to armbar by controlling their wrist and swinging your leg over their head; (2) transition to omoplata by releasing the triangle lock and rotating your hips to control their arm in the omoplata configuration; (3) if they extract their arm and posture, use the scramble to recover to closed guard or half guard; (4) if they drive into you to pass, use the leg positioning to establish rubber guard or mission control. The triangle attempt itself creates reactions that feed secondary attacks.

knowledge_assessment.question: What physical attribute is most important for executing this triangle from Crackhead Control, and why?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Hip mobility and explosive hip power are the most critical attributes, more than leg length or flexibility. The entire entry depends on generating sufficient rotational force from the hips to create space for leg insertion while simultaneously disrupting the opponent's base. Practitioners with shorter legs can compensate with superior hip rotation and timing, but no amount of leg length compensates for insufficient hip explosiveness. Conditioning for repeated explosive hip movements from turtle position should be a training priority.

safety_considerations: The Triangle Choke creates bilateral compression of the carotid arteries, which can cause loss of consciousness within 8-12 seconds of a properly applied choke. Partners must tap early and clearly when they feel the choke tighten. The attacking practitioner must release immediately upon feeling or hearing the tap - there is no safe margin for holding a blood choke after the tap signal. During drilling, apply the choke slowly and incrementally to allow your partner to tap before full compression. The hip rotation entry from turtle carries risk of neck strain if the bottom player's head is trapped during the explosive movement. Ensure your head is free before committing to the rotation. Avoid cranking the neck or applying twisting pressure to the cervical spine - the triangle should compress the sides of the neck, not torque the spine. Practitioners with pre-existing neck injuries should approach this technique with caution and consult with their instructor before attempting the entry from turtle position.
position_integration: The Triangle Choke from Crackhead Control represents a critical offensive weapon within the 10th Planet turtle defense system. It transforms Crackhead Control bottom from a purely defensive survival position into a legitimate submission threat, forcing top players to respect offensive possibilities even from inferior positions. Within the broader BJJ positional hierarchy, this technique connects the turtle/Crackhead Control defensive system to the triangle attack chain (triangle to armbar to omoplata), creating a complete offensive pathway from what most practitioners consider a purely defensive position. The technique integrates with Mission Control, Crackhead Control, and other 10th Planet rubber guard positions that emphasize leg-based control and submissions from bottom. It also serves as a psychological deterrent - opponents who know you threaten triangles from turtle will modify their top turtle attacks, potentially creating openings for other escapes like granby rolls or sit-throughs.
